title: Speech Writing — salutation, hooks, persuasive devices
notes: **What it is:** writing meant to be SPOKEN — short sentences, rhythm, direct address. The examiner checks 'speakability'.

**Structure:** Salutation in order of seniority ('Respected Chairperson, judges, teachers, and my dear friends —') → Self-intro (if required) → Hook (question/fact/quotation) → 2–3 clear points ('First… Second… Finally…') → Persuasive devices (triads, repetition, rhetorical questions) → Strong closing appeal + 'Thank you.'
**Grammar for the ear:** imperatives command action ('Let us pledge…'); rhetorical questions make the audience answer mentally; triads create rhythm.
**Test:** read your draft aloud — where you gasp, rewrite. Repeat your core phrase 2–3 times.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

**Complete speech template:**
[Salutation — seniority order: 'Respected Chairperson, distinguished judges, learned teachers, and my dear friends –']

[Self-introduction (if required): 'My name is… from Class… I stand before you today to speak about…']

[Hook: A striking fact, a powerful question, or a memorable quotation]

[Point 1: 'Let me begin with…' / 'First, let me tell you…']

[Point 2: 'Secondly…' / 'But there's more…']

[Point 3: 'Finally…' / 'And most importantly…']

[Closing: Emotional appeal + call to action + 'Thank you.']

**Salutation — the etiquette of order:** Speeches in exams always start with a salutation listing people in ORDER OF SENIORITY: (1) Chairperson/Principal → (2) Judges → (3) Teachers → (4) Fellow students → (5) Guests. Example: 'Respected Chairperson, learned judges, dear teachers, and my fellow students — Good morning to you all.' Do NOT skip anyone mentioned in the prompt. Do NOT reorder them. The salutation shows respect and awareness of protocol.

**Self-introduction — when and how:** Include only if the question says 'introduce yourself'. If required: 'My name is Ram from Class 11-A. Today I wish to speak about…' Keep it to ONE sentence. If not required, skip it — wasting words on self-intro eats into your argument time. In formal speech competitions, the introduction comes after the hook; in exams, before.

**Speech hooks — grab attention in the first 10 seconds:** (1) *Rhetorical question*: 'What would you do if you lost everything today?' (2) *Startling fact*: 'One billion people globally go to bed hungry every night.' (3) *Quotation*: 'Mahatma Gandhi once said,

But how many of us actually try?' (4) *Direct address*: 'Look around you. What do you see?' (5) *Story*: 'Last Tuesday, a five-year-old girl in a remote village walked 10 kilometres to school. Her name is Sita.' (6) *Quote with twist*: 'They say knowledge is power. But I say knowledge without action is merely information.' Pick the hook that best suits your topic's tone.

**Speech body — three points max:** You have about 2-3 minutes in a speech. Cover 2-3 points maximum. Each point should: (1) Have a clear heading signal ('First…', 'Second…', 'Finally…'); (2) Explain one idea with a short example or story; (3) Connect back to your main argument. Never try to cover 5 topics in 200 words. Depth beats breadth every time in speech writing.

**Persuasive devices — the orator's toolkit:** (1) *Triads* (rule of three): 'Education builds character, creates opportunity, and transforms communities.' (2) *Repetition*: 'We must act now. We must act together. We must act with conviction.' (3) *Rhetorical questions*: 'Is this the Nepal we want for our children?' (4) *Direct address*: 'You have the power to change this. YOU have the responsibility.' (5) *Triadic structure*: 'Not because it is easy, but because it is necessary.' (6) *Anaphora*: 'I dream of a Nepal… I dream of a generation… I dream of a future…' These devices create rhythm, emphasis, and memorability.

**Speech vs. Essay — the fundamental difference:** An essay is READ; a speech is HEARD. This changes everything. Speech sentences should be SHORTER (15-20 words maximum). Use MORE contractions ('don't', 'it's', 'we'll') — speech is oral, not written. Use MORE repetition — the audience can't go back and re-read. Use MORE direct address ('you', 'we') — the speaker is talking TO people. Use LESS complex subordinate clauses — keep the grammar simple and clear.

**The read-aloud test — your best editing tool:** After writing your speech, read it ALOUD to yourself. Mark anywhere you: (1) Run out of breath — split that sentence; (2) Stumble over words — rephrase; (3) Feel bored — add emotion or a question; (4) Lose the audience's attention — cut that sentence. A speech that reads well on paper but sounds awkward when spoken is a failed speech. This test catches 80% of speech-writing errors.

**Closing a speech — the power moment:** The last 20 seconds determine how your speech is remembered. Close with: (1) *Call to action*: 'Let us all pledge to plant one tree this month.' (2) *Rhetorical question*: 'What legacy do you want to leave?' (3) *Repetition of theme*: 'Education is not just a right. Education is a revolution. Education is hope.' (4) *Quotation*: End with a powerful quote that reinforces your message. (5) *Final 'Thank you'*: Always end with 'Thank you.' — it signals the speech is over and allows applause.

**Speech vocabulary — power phrases for oratory:** Opening: 'I stand before you today to…', 'Let me begin by asking…', 'How many of you have ever…' Body: 'Consider this…', 'Think about…', 'Picture this…', 'Let me give you an example…', 'Here's the thing…' Closing: 'Let us not forget…', 'The choice is ours…', 'Together, we can…', 'I urge you all to…', 'Thank you for your time and attention.'

**Common speech writing mistakes:** (1) No salutation or wrong order. (2) Starting with 'Good morning everyone' without listing dignitaries first. (3) Long, complex sentences that are hard to speak. (4) No rhetorical devices — dry and forgettable. (5) No clear call to action. (6) Ending abruptly without 'Thank you.' (7) Too formal — 'One should consider the implications…' (8) Too casual — 'So basically, stuff is bad.' (9) Ignoring the given first line (if provided). (10) Over-running the word limit.

**Speech delivery tips (for oral exams):** Make eye contact with different sections of the audience. Vary your tone — don't speak in a monotone. Pause after important points. Use hand gestures naturally. Speak slowly and clearly. Breathe between sentences. Smile when appropriate. Your BODY LANGUAGE matters as much as your words. A confident delivery can turn an average speech into a winning one.
confusion: Speech vs. Essay — key structural differences: Speeches have salutations, direct address ('you', 'we'), shorter sentences, repetition, and rhetorical devices. Essays have no salutation, use 'one/it is said', longer sentences, logical transitions, and no repetition. Don't write a speech like an essay, or an essay like a speech.

Rhetorical question vs. Direct question: A rhetorical question ('Have you ever felt truly alone?') does NOT expect an answer — it makes the audience THINK. A direct question ('How many students feel alone?') expects a show of hands or verbal response. In speech writing, rhetorical questions are the standard tool. Direct questions sound interrogative and aggressive.

Quotation in speech vs. quotation in essay: In a speech, quotations are SPOKEN — keep them short (one sentence max) and deliver them with emphasis. In an essay, quotations can be longer and embedded in analysis. Also: in a speech, introduce the quotation ('As the great Dr. Koirala said…') before delivering it. In an essay, you can weave it into your sentence.

Point of view in speech vs. narrative: Speeches use 'I' (speaker) and 'you' (audience) and 'we' (shared identity). Narratives use 'I' or 'he/she' but NOT 'you' (unless second-person narrative, which is rare). The speech 'you' creates intimacy; the narrative 'you' creates confusion. Never write 'You walked into the room and felt scared' in a speech.

Thank you placement — before or after closing point: In a speech, 'Thank you' is the ABSOLUTE LAST WORD. It comes after your closing appeal, not before. Correct: 'Let us act together. Thank you.' Incorrect: 'Thank you. Let us act together.' The final words must carry your message, not your politeness.
practice: Write a speech (200-220 words) on 'The Power of Reading in the Digital Age'. Include: full salutation, self-introduction, a hook (quotation or rhetorical question), three clear points with transition signals, at least two persuasive devices (triad + repetition), and a strong call-to-action closing ending with 'Thank you.'

Write a speech (180-200 words) on 'Why Every Student Should Volunteer at Least Once'. Use: a rhetorical question as your hook, three points with first/second/final signals, a triad in your closing appeal, and direct address ('you', 'we') throughout. Read it aloud and mark where you need to pause.

Rewrite this paragraph as a speech excerpt, converting it from essay to oral style: 'It is imperative that educational institutions recognise the significance of practical learning experiences as opposed to purely theoretical instruction.' Then explain three specific changes you made and why.

Write a speech (200 words) beginning with the given line: 'Standing here today, I am reminded of a simple truth — the greatest tool a human being possesses is not technology, but the human mind.' Continue the speech on the topic of 'The Importance of Critical Thinking'. Include a quotation, a rhetorical question, and a closing appeal.

Critique this speech opening: 'Respected teachers, good morning. I am going to talk about pollution. Pollution is a big problem. It affects everyone. We should do something about it.' List at least five errors and rewrite the opening correctly.
universalFacts: The art of public speaking (rhetoric) was systematised by the ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle in his work 'Rhetoric' (350 BCE). He identified three modes of persuasion: ethos (credibility), pathos (emotion), and logos (logic). Every successful speech uses all three — credibility, emotional appeal, and logical argument.

In the NEB English exam, speech writing carries 8-10 marks. The marking scheme prioritises: salutation format (2 marks), content and organisation (4 marks), language and expression (3 marks), and persuasive devices (1 mark). Missing the salutation or ending without 'Thank you' are the most common format errors.

Studies in communication show that the average human attention span for a spoken presentation is 10-15 minutes. In exams, a 200-250 word speech takes approximately 2-3 minutes to deliver at a natural speaking pace (130-150 words per minute). This is why conciseness is a virtue in speech writing.

The 'rule of three' (triads) is one of the most powerful techniques in oratory, used by speakers from Abraham Lincoln to Martin Luther King Jr. ('Government of the people, by the people, for the people'). The human brain finds patterns of three satisfying and memorable — 'life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness' has greater impact than 'life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness, and justice.'

The most effective speeches follow a simple pattern: (1) HOOK — grab attention immediately, (2) PROBLEM — explain why the audience should care, (3) SOLUTION — offer a clear path forward, (4) CALL TO ACTION — tell the audience exactly what to do. This pattern works for persuasive, inspirational, and informational speeches alike.
